items.headline: Am I Audio launch I Am Choir
items.body_text:
Following years of development, Am I Audio have just officially launched their debut plug-in. Created in collaboration with Tokyo-based music technology experts Neurotone, Inc., I Am Choir is capable of turning a single vocal track into a full choral arrangement while preserving the original words and melody of the original part.

The company say that the plug-in should be thought of as a “timbre transfer” processor rather than a composition or lyric-writing tool. They liken it to the way an amp simulator works, but rather than signals emerging sounding as if they’ve been played through and amp, they come out sounding like they’ve been sung by a choir! As well as generating multiple voices, I Am Choir includes a harmony engine that’s capable of adding parts either a third or a fifth above or below the input melody, with users able to select the relevant scale and key.

There are no cloud-based services involved — all of the plug-in’s processing takes place natively on the user’s computer.

Three Choirs

The new arrival was created in partnership with three groups of singers, all of whom contributed their voices knowingly and consensually, and have received both compensation for their work and been provided with royalties on the plug-in. Here’s what’s included:

Gospel Choir: Trained in partnership with a Los Angeles gospel choir, coordinated by Eric Howard.

Kids' Choir: Trained in partnership with MUSYCA Children's Choir

Shout: Trained with singers from Am I Audio’s personal network of artists, writers and producers

Ethical AI

Here is Am I Audio’s statement on their use of AI:

“Am I Audio are a team of lifelong musicians, songwriters, and producers. We built this I Am Choir, a first-of-its-kind AI choir plug-in, from inside the process, as people who deeply understand what it means to create, collaborate, and try to bring forward what is missing in the world.

“I Am Choir was built in direct collaboration with incredible singers. Every voice was contributed knowingly, consensually and ethically. The singers involved were compensated for their work and will share in the success of the tool through a royalty.

“We believe nothing will ever replace the magic of humans singing together in a room. This tool is not a replacement for that experience. It is an expansion of what is possible.

“Think of the first time you heard Pink Floyd, ‘Another brick wall pt. 2’ or Justice, ‘D.A.N.C.E’ or Gucci Mane, ‘Lemonade’, and felt immediately inspired to write a chorus for a kids’ choir.

“Our goal is to give artists access to sounds, ideas and workflows that were previously inaccessible due to cost, logistics or geography, while honouring the people whose voices make those sounds possible.”

Compatibility

I Am Choir is supported on Macs running macOS 12 or later, with Windows support currently in development. VST3, AU and AAX plug-in versions are available.

Pricing & Availability

I Am Choir is available now, and is being offered at an introductory price of $169 (usually $199) until 1 September 2026.

images.cap: Am I Audio I Am Choir AI vocal ensemble virtual instrument plug-in

items.headline: Push Hack, very unauthorized access to Push 3’s display, files, MIDI, and more
items.body_text:
If you don’t like unauthorized hacking, this isn’t for you. If you don’t like things built with AI-assisted coding agents, this isn’t for you. But if you’re up for a very unofficial hack that gives you full takeover access to Push 3’s display, drives, MIDI, and more, Federico Pepe has just unveiled Push Hack.

Here’s the idea: you use an SSH (secure shell) connection to Push 3 standalone — which is, after all, a Linux computer under the hood — and install modular hacks. It’s a proof of concept, but it does demonstrate what Ableton could do officially. And I hope that we see some official support along similar lines.

And Federico Pepe is deeply involved with Ableton Live as a certified trainer and brand manager. You may know him as “the guy who hacked Flappy Bird and Doom so they run inside Ableton Live’s Extensions.” See below.

Modules at launch:

Push Manager for uploading, managing, and downloading files and projects à la Move Manager.

USB drive support over the USB-A connection.

Full display takeover, including draw and uploading images and videos. (So you can’t play Doom yet, but you could at least run a video of someone playing Doom… or Marathon, or whatever.)

Full MIDI takeover. I really wanted this as a launch feature: full control of every push, pad, and control with bidirectional feedback (see details below).

LED control, reverse-engineered with every color and animation.

System stats: CPU, memory, disk, IP addresses, hotspot password. (That sounds like a security hole, but it’s not — you’re giving yourself SSH access. Anyone with SSH access before already had full access to the device.)

The MIDI takeover mode is what is perhaps most compelling. Federico tells CDM:

With the “Intercept” mode enabled, messages from Push are read but not forwarded to Push’s software, so you can use buttons, knobs, etc to control things without triggering anything on the main software. I also added a “Forward” mode, so all the MIDI messages are automatically forwarded to the MIDI out port (without any routing inside the Push UI).

And there’s the chance to do more, he says: “Because I have full control of MIDI, Screen and LED, I built a “Shadow UI” that is layered on top of Push’s UI. The idea is to go beyond Push Manager and do everything on Push itself.”

I expect this won’t make the same splash that the Ableton Move hacks did, just because there aren’t as many standalone units out there (at least to my knowledge), and, while far more powerful, this is also more complex.

I suppose the impact of AI could make vendors lock down systems — or, at the other extreme, just assume users will go hack them themselves. But I do hope these kind of experiments suggest something else: it’d be great to have a supported API for the devices we own, so they are open to greater customization. That isn’t always an easy engineering task, so I get that there’s investment involved. But in the end, it could mean architectures that are more flexible for the vendor and third parties alike. And where we’ve seen these kinds of tools — officially and unofficially on Move, in custom SDKs from Novation, in hacks like this, and in more open boutique platforms like those from monome — user communities have done amazing things. The investment is real, but so is the return.

Anyway, that mini-diatribe aside, I’ll be curious what happens with this. And this kind of reverse-engineering task is something machine learning is really good at — including when those applications are far from benign, so be ready. (This is why July became my “let’s look at server threat mediation month,” if anyone wants to nerd out about something not directly music tech-related, but very necessary to survival on the internet!)

Thanks, Federico.

Push 3 hardware display taken over to show a live MIDI monitor
Push 3 running the Push Hack MIDI monitor module
Reverse-engineered LED control lighting Push 3’s pads in every colour
Push Hack automation lanes view rendered on the Push 3 display

items.headline: Spotify expands AI remix and covers project with Merlin partnership
items.body_text:
During its second-quarter earnings call on Tuesday, Spotify again teased the upcoming release of a new product that will allow music fans to leverage AI to make covers and remixes of artists’ music, with the artists’ consent.

The company also announced that Merlin, a licensing partner for independent labels and distributors, has now joined Universal Music Group (UMG) on the new AI music effort. The deal brings more than 30,000 labels from Merlin’s network to the product, which will allow fan-made covers and remixes by artists who agree to participate.

Spotify has positioned its AI music product as being significantly different from the more controversial AI music startups that have been used to create fully artificial songs. Instead, Spotify co-CEO Gustav Söderström told investors on Tuesday’s call that the company’s AI music product will be about “real artists, not fake artists.”

“We want artists to be consenting [to add] their work into this catalog, so people can play around with covers and remixes based on their art,” added co-CEO Alex Norström. “We also obviously want to give them credit. And last but not least…we not only have the consent and give credit, but we also drive the compensation for this. So, really, we’re talking about the first legal way to partake in this AI tailwind that we see coming for interactive music,” he said.

AI music has flooded streaming services. Music streamer Deezer recently noted that more than 50% of daily track uploads were generated with AI, up from 10% in January 2025.

The company told investors that a research preview of the fan remix and covers product would initially be made available to a subset of users. Spotify also noted that it would not require a full music catalog to get started. The company did not say when the preview would arrive.

The new tool will launch as a paid add-on, creating an additional revenue stream for artists, Spotify previously said.

“Our remix and covers I think is an incredibly exciting product again because there is no one else that can really do this,” Söderström said. “Normal generative music will happen with or without us. This product will not happen without us, and it needs to exist so that existing artists can participate in this.”

images.cap: Spotify logo on a phone screen. Image Credits: Klaudia Radecka/NurPhoto / Getty Images

items.headline: Suno Vinyl: Press Your AI-Generated Music to Vinyl
items.body_text:
The AI Music platform is starting a vinyl pressing and shipping service.

Suno Vinyl is coming soon, giving you the ability to turn your Suno library tracklist into a unique 12-inch record with a custom-designed sleeve.

Suno is an AI music platform that instantly generates full tracks laden with vocals and instruments using nothing more than basic text prompts. The freemium tier structure gives you different plans with monthly credits to generate tracks, and you can then extend sections, remix, or separate stems from the results.

Suno Vinyl

With Suno’s Vinyl pressing service, you’ll be able to bring your creations to life in the form of a custom 12-inch, pressed and printed by Suno and shipped to a location of your choice. The simple three-step process starts with selecting the tracks from your personal Suno library, for a tracklist with a total of 46 minutes.

The next step involves uploading your colour album artwork for the custom record sleeve and the labels on either side of the record, and finally, the record is pressed, passed through quality control, and then shipped. The record itself is made from polyethylene terephthalate glycol (PETG) vinyl, which is both durable and eco-friendly.

Although Suno stipulates on its website that the pressing process starts with tracks in your personal Suno library, it’s unclear whether or not you’ll be able to press vinyl from uploaded tracks that weren’t generated with Suno AI. Regardless, there are still ways that you could use this process creatively.

For example, if you filled the record with stems, beats, drum breaks, and other material with the intention of resampling the audio and capturing the sound of vinyl, it becomes a creative tool in your sample-based music production process. Naturally, the audio can be chopped up and used freely, without ever worrying about sample clearance or impending lawsuits.

Pricing and Availability:

According to the official website, the Suno Vinyl pressing service will cost approximately $45 per record, excluding shipping.

images.cap: Suno Vinyl: Press Your AI-Generated Music to Vinyl
Suno Vinyl custom 12-inch record and sleeve

items.headline: Key EU AI Act rules now being enforced – so how does that affect the music industry?
items.body_text:
On Sunday 2 August, the EU Artificial Intelligence Act was beefed-up – with a set of key consumer-facing transparency rules, AI compliance requirements, and regulatory enforcement powers all coming into force. There are a lot of facets to this act, and in terms of it impacting you or your work, it’s most likely that it will affect the tools you are already using – but there are some key ways in which it may affect the music industry. We’ve rounded up some of the main points for you to digest:

Transparency and labelling

One now-enforceable element that we’re already seeing reflected across DSPs is connected to the act’s public transparency and mandatory labelling mandate: AI-generated or modified images, audio, video, and text must now carry visible labels. They must also have embedded, machine-readable watermarks so that platforms (and users) can easily detect AI content. In recent weeks, we’ve seen the emergence of new systems for labelling AI-generated music and AI ‘Proof of Human’ fingerprinting startups like Genotone.

Comprehensive summaries of datasets used for training

Here’s a demand made by Article 53 of the EU law that might have more far-reaching consequences: platforms that the the EU calls “General-Purpose AI” or GPAI (i.e. big ones that are trained on massive, broad datasets, like OpenAI, or Udio) must now maintain technical documentation and publish summaries of training data. Read in a simple sense, this means that companies deploying GPAI music models in the EU will need to publish a comprehensive summary of the datasets – i.e. listing the songs! – used during training. But will they? So far, many AI music companies have resisted this.

The music industry, which has set out principles governing AI regulation, won lawsuits in Germany against Suno and been pressing for data transparency, will be keenly investigating how this rule could help their cause. European judges can now compel AI developers to produce their EU AI Act-mandated documentation during, for example, court discovery in a legal case: it’ll be interesting to see if and how this part of the law might be used.

Opt-out policies

The industry has been wrestling over the opt-in vs opt-out approach with regards to the use of composers’ and performers’ work in AI models. Here’s what the EU AI law says: GPAI developers need to establish policies that detect, respect, and enforce rightsholders’ opt-outs. That means that when rightholders place digital opt-out metadata onto a song, AI companies cannot legally train their models on those tracks for the EU market without a paid license.

All of the above is enforced with some stiff fines, and potential platform bans within the EU. As we said at the beginning, we’re seeing changes that are in line with these laws already – and perhaps it will expedite the emergence of fully-licensed genAI music models. It’s affecting music businesses directly, too: UMG’s 2025 annual financial filings flagged potentially “significant obligations and costs related to monitoring and compliance” relating to laws like the EU AI Act.

If you’d like to get up to speed further, this plain-language EU AI Act compliance guide is a good starting point – and has article-by-article breakdowns, plus compliance checklists.

images.cap: EU flag illustration accompanying Music Ally's EU AI Act explainer
